lessons.title: Looking after new seedlings
lessons.html:
Looking after new seedlings

In the nursery we grow flowers like petunias, marigolds and alyssum from seed. The seeds are sown in seed trays. When the small plants come up, they are called seedlings. New seedlings are weak. They need your care every day.

What young seedlings need

  • Water. Keep the mix damp, but not wet. Use a fine rose on the can or a fine mist. A strong jet of water knocks seedlings over.
  • Light. Seedlings need good light. With too little light they grow tall and thin and fall over. Too much hot sun can burn them.
  • Warmth. Keep them out of cold wind. In winter they stay in the tunnel or greenhouse.
  • Air. Fresh air helps stop fungus. Open the tunnel sides on warm days if your supervisor says so.

Daily checks

  1. Feel the mix with your finger. Is it dry? Then water gently.
  2. Look at the seedlings. Are they standing up and green?
  3. Look for seedlings that fall over at the bottom of the stem. This is called damping off. It is a fungus. Tell your supervisor at once.
  4. Look for snails, slugs, cutworms or ants.
  5. Check that the label is still in the tray.

Watering the right way

Water early in the morning. Then the leaves dry during the day. Wet leaves at night help fungus to grow. Do not let water stand in the tray. Make sure the tray has holes so extra water can run out.

Never leave trays to dry out on a hot day. One hot afternoon without water can kill a whole tray.

lessons.title: Growing on and pricking out
lessons.html:
Growing on and pricking out

After a few weeks the seedlings get their first true leaves. The first two small leaves are seed leaves. The next leaves are true leaves. They look like the leaves of the grown plant. Now the seedlings are ready to be pricked out.

What is pricking out?

Pricking out means lifting each small seedling out of the seed tray and planting it in its own space. This can be a cell in a seedling tray, a small pot or a pack. Each plant now has more room to grow.

Getting ready

  • Fill clean trays or pots with fresh growing mix. Firm it gently.
  • Water the seed tray an hour before so the mix is soft.
  • Make a small hole in each cell with a dibber or a stick.
  • Work in the shade, not in hot sun or wind.

How to prick out

  1. Loosen the seedlings with the dibber.
  2. Hold the seedling by a leaf, never by the stem. A leaf can grow again. A broken stem kills the plant.
  3. Lift it out with its roots.
  4. Put it in the hole. The roots must go straight down.
  5. Press the mix around it gently.
  6. Water with a fine rose.
  7. Put a label in the tray: plant name, colour and date.

After pricking out

Keep the new trays in light shade for a few days. The plants need time to grow new roots. Then move them to their normal place. Throw away weak or sick seedlings. Only plant strong ones.

Work fast and carefully. Seedlings left lying on the bench dry out in minutes.

lessons.title: Growing to transplant size and controlling pests
lessons.html:
Growing to transplant size and controlling pests

After pricking out, the plants grow on until they are big enough to sell or to plant in the garden. This is called transplanting maturity.

Caring for growing plants

  • Water every day if needed. Check the cells in the middle and at the edges of the tray.
  • Feed the plants with fertiliser only as your supervisor tells you. Too much fertiliser burns the roots.
  • Space trays so air can move and each plant gets light.
  • Pull out weeds while they are small.

When is a plant ready?

A plant is ready when:

  • The roots fill the cell and hold the mix together.
  • The plant has several healthy true leaves.
  • It is strong, green and not too tall.

Before plants go outside, harden them off. Put them in more sun and wind for some days. Then they will not get a shock when they are planted.

Pests in seedlings

PestWhat you see
Snails and slugsHoles in leaves, shiny slime trails
AphidsSmall green or black insects on new leaves
CutwormsPlants cut off at soil level
WhiteflyTiny white flies when you shake the plant

What to do

  1. Check plants every day.
  2. Pick off snails and cutworms by hand.
  3. Remove and throw away badly sick plants.
  4. Tell your supervisor what you found and where.

Only a trained person may spray chemicals. Never spray without permission, the right protective clothing and the label instructions. Never eat or drink when working with chemicals. Wash your hands after work.

Key points

  • Water gently, in the morning, and never let trays dry out.
  • Prick out when the first true leaves show; hold seedlings by a leaf.
  • Label every tray with name, colour and date.
  • A plant is ready when roots fill the cell; harden it off first.
  • Check for pests every day and report them; do not spray unless trained.
